solution_summary.rationale: The bottleneck state shows purely compute-bound FFN1 tilings (99.99% compute time, 98.4% compute energy) with 4096 compute units per WS chiplet. Each of the 16 FFN1 tilings consumes ~14.5B latency on its assigned chiplet via tensor_parall=16. Increasing compute_units from 4096 to 16384 reduces FFN1 latency by ~4x (to ~3.6B per tiling), cutting critical path latency from ~29.1B to ~18.2B. Compute energy scales proportionally with compute time, so energy also decreases significantly. Although monetary cost will increase (compute cost is 49.3% of total), the combined latency-energy reduction is substantial enough to plausibly compensate. No historical cases exist to contradict this direction. The candidate was materialized via modify_hardware_parameter and is ready for evaluation.

rationale: The best configuration (iteration 3, objective 8.49e26) has 32 WS chiplets at max compute_units (16384) with 8192 buffer. The primary bottleneck is compute-bound FFN1 layers (68.4% of time, 99.9% compute, 2.84s each). compute_units is already at the legal maximum (16384), so the remaining compute lever is buffer_size. Increasing buffer_size from 8192 to 32768 enables better tiling for the large FFN1 GEMMs, reducing compute time per tiling. The critical-path tail (norm2/res2) is memory/communication-bound but has tiny latency (11.9M vs 153.5B total). The DRAM BW increase (64->128) already failed (5.5% objective worsening) because the MC increase (+6.4%) outweighed the tiny latency/energy gains. buffer_size is a per-chiplet storage parameter whose cost is embedded in the compute cost component (52.8% of MC), so the MC impact is expected to be minimal. This is a low-risk, targeted move that directly addresses the primary compute bottleneck.

llm_notes.history_usage: Retrieved cases showed: (1) compute_units increase from 4096 to 16384 on 16 chiplets improved objective by 54% (iteration 0->1), confirming compute capacity is the key bottleneck. (2) NoP BW increase from 128 to 256 on 16 chiplets worsened objective by 73% due to MC doubling (iteration 1->2). (3) DRAM BW increase from 64 to 128 on 32 chiplets worsened objective by 5.5% (iteration 3->4). These negative cases argue against repeating bandwidth increases. (4) num_chiplets increase from 16 to 32 improved objective by 12% (iteration 1->3), but further chiplet increases would significantly increase OS cost (39.4% of MC). The buffer_size increase is a novel direction not yet explored in any retrieved case.
llm_notes.cost_risk: Monetary cost is expected to increase minimally or stay flat. buffer_size is a per-chiplet storage parameter whose cost is embedded in the compute cost component (52.8% of MC). The OS cost (39.4%) and IO cost (7.9%) remain unchanged. The expected latency reduction from better tiling should compensate for any small MC increase.

dram_bw increase (64->128): already tried on 32 chiplets, 5.5% objective worsening
num_chiplets increase (32->64): would significantly increase OS cost (39.4% of MC) with uncertain latency benefit
micro_batch increase (2->4): zero MC impact but may have diminishing returns since FFN1 layers already fully utilize all 32 chiplets; could be explored later

llm_notes.risk: The main risk is that increasing buffer_size from 8192 to 32768 may not significantly reduce compute time for the FFN1 tilings if the tiling is already optimal at 8192. The compute-bound FFN1 layers have 99.9% compute time share, suggesting the compute array is fully saturated regardless of buffer size. However, larger buffers can enable better data reuse and reduce DRAM access for weight matrices, potentially reducing compute time indirectly. The MC impact is expected to be minimal, so even a small latency reduction would improve the combined objective.
